title: Headaches in several family members in winter — focused assessment, critical decision and communication

blocks.text: Headaches in several family members in winter — focused assessment, critical decision and communication
AMaC MRCP PACES23 | R5-227 | Station 2: Acute consultation | Skills A–G; appropriate clinical assessment | 20 minutes | AMaC educational mark grid, not official MRCP(UK) marks.

Two adults and a child in one household have morning headaches, nausea and dizziness that improve when they leave home. Take a focused history and explain your immediate plan. A nurse can provide observations or blood results on request.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: Hook: Suspected carbon monoxide exposure. Trap: Multiple co-located headaches suggest an environmental toxin: ordinary pulse oximetry cannot exclude carbon monoxide.

rows: “Before anything else, I need to check whether you are seriously unwell.”
“I have a few specific questions to help work out the cause.”

Ask about gas boilers, heaters, fires, other affected people or pets and temporal relation to being indoors. Assess airway, neurological status, pregnancy and chest pain; do not rely on a normal pulse oximeter.
“I am concerned about a potentially serious condition.”
“I will explain the tests and what happens next.”

Immediately move everyone into fresh air; contact emergency services, provide high-concentration oxygen and urgent assessment. Send carboxyhaemoglobin via blood co-oximetry without delaying oxygen; consider ECG and troponin, and specialist advice for severe poisoning or pregnancy.

blocks.text: You are frightened and ask “Can I go home?” Give the opening complaint spontaneously; answer focused questions consistently with examiner findings. Ask one question about long-term consequences or family safety as appropriate.

Q1: What finding is diagnostic clue?
Expected answer: Several cohabitants symptomatic in winter, especially with improvement outside.

Q2: What immediate instruction?
Expected answer: Leave exposure site, call emergency help, do not re-enter until safe.

Q3: Will pulse oximetry exclude CO toxicity?
Expected answer: No, standard SpO2 readings may be normal despite significant CO poisoning.

Q4: What laboratory testing?
Expected answer: COHb measured by co-oximetry; clinical decisions should not rest on COHb alone.

Q5: What hospital treatment?
Expected answer: High-concentration oxygen, monitoring and specialist advice for severe exposure or pregnancy.

THINK: Suspected carbon monoxide exposure. SAY: acknowledge uncertainty. DO: Immediately move everyone into fresh air; contact emergency services, provide high-concentration oxygen and urgent assessment. Send carboxyhaemoglobin via blood co-oximetry without delaying oxygen; consider ECG and troponin, and specialist advice for severe poisoning or pregnancy. NUMBERS: 20-minute PACES encounter. TRAP: Multiple co-located headaches suggest an environmental toxin: ordinary pulse oximetry cannot exclude carbon monoxide. FINISH: Carboxyhaemoglobin concentration may fall after oxygen and does not alone determine severity. Do not let any household member re-enter until the supply has been declared safe by appropriate responders.
